events.title: Romania says it stopped Russian cyberattack targeting government emails

articles.text: Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, speaks in Bucharest during a meeting with Romanian President Nicușor Dan. Credit: European Union Romania says it stopped Russian cyberattack targeting government emails Romania's intelligence agency said it stopped a cyberattack by Russian state-linked hackers on a government institution late last year. The cyberespionage campaign was revealed earlier this week by researchers who found the group targeted Romania in an attempt to intercept emails exchanged with NATO and European Union institutions. The Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said Wednesday that it detected the intrusion in December 2025 and took steps to contain the attack and restore the affected systems. The operation was attributed to Turla, a long-running Russian cyberespionage group linked to Moscow's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to the agency, the hackers exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft systems but Romanian cybersecurity specialists managed to stop the attack. "No exfiltration of sensitive data was identified," the agency said, adding that the affected email service had been restored. The SRI did not identify the targeted government institution or provide details about how the hackers initially gained access. The Slovak cybersecurity firm ESET said Turla used a previously unknown hacking toolkit to compromise government email servers in Romania and Kazakhstan. The malware, dubbed Cereal, allowed attackers to secretly monitor email traffic, collect selected messages and maintain access to compromised Microsoft Exchange servers while avoiding detection. In Romania, the malware was specifically configured to intercept emails sent to or received from NATO and EU institutions, according to ESET. A NATO and EU member bordering Ukraine and Moldova, Romania has repeatedly warned of Russian cyberattacks and other hybrid threats. The country has also reported incidents involving Russian drones entering or approaching its airspace during Moscow's attacks on Ukraine. The SRI said it had informed relevant Romanian authorities about the incident and shared information with European intelligence services and partners within NATO and the EU. Romanian authorities are also investigating other potentially related cyber operations linked to Russia, the agency said. Turla — also known as Secret Blizzard and Venomous Bear — has operated for more than two decades and is considered one of Russia's most established cyberespionage groups. It has previously targeted government agencies, diplomatic missions and defense organizations across Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East. In July, a cyberattack disrupted Romania's national land registry system, taking critical digital services offline in what the agency responsible for the system described as the most serious technical incident in its history. Earlier this year, Romania's then-defense minister warned that government institutions were facing thousands of attempted cyberattacks every day, many of them suspected of originating from Russia. events.title: Poland shuts down government services platform ePUAP following cyberattack

articles.text: Image: Polina Kuzikova via Unsplash Poland shuts down government services platform ePUAP following cyberattack Poland temporarily shut down a government platform used by citizens and businesses to access public services after detecting and stopping a cyberattack, officials said Tuesday. The attack targeted ePUAP, a nationwide system that allows users to submit official documents, communicate with government agencies and complete administrative procedures online. Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said security teams responded immediately to the incident and were working to restore the platform's full functionality. "The cyberattack on the state ePUAP system was detected and stopped," Gawkowski said in a social media post. The minister said the infrastructure of Poland's Central Information Technology Center, the government agency responsible for maintaining key digital services, including ePUAP, remained secure. Officials said the ePUAP platform was taken offline as a precaution rather than because of damage caused by the attack. "It's not that the system was somehow compromised or its operation was disrupted by this attack," Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told Polish news agency PAP. "We simply disabled it as a precautionary measure." Authorities have not disclosed how the attack was carried out or who was responsible. There has been no public confirmation that hackers gained access to government systems or stole sensitive information. The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring the platform, saying services will resume once security specialists complete their work. According to a notice on the government's website, ePUAP electronic mailboxes remain unavailable to citizens and public institutions. The disruption could also temporarily affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which allows people to access public services and electronically sign official documents. Poland has faced repeated cyberattacks targeting government institutions, critical infrastructure and private companies in recent months. In October, Polish online invoicing provider Fakturownia reported a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners. In September, hackers also stole data from Qbusoft, a Polish healthcare software provider, following a separate breach involving medical technology company MyDr. Polish authorities said the MyDr incident potentially affected information relating to about 19 million people and roughly 12,000 healthcare organizations.
